Casino Bonus Wagering Requirements Explained

Published August 31, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

"Deposit $100, get $100 free" reads like the whole deal, but it almost never is. Nearly every online casino bonus comes attached to a wagering requirement — a rule that decides how much you have to bet before any of that bonus money, or the winnings it produces, can actually be withdrawn. Two offers that look identical on the surface can be worth wildly different amounts once that requirement is factored in. This guide breaks down how wagering requirements are structured, how to calculate what one actually costs you, and the fine print that trips people up most often. Nothing here refers to any specific operator's current offer — the terms below are the general mechanics you'll find across the industry, and every real bonus should be checked against its own written terms before you rely on any of it.

What a wagering requirement actually is

A wagering requirement — also called a playthrough or rollover requirement — is the total amount you must wager before bonus funds (and often the winnings generated from them) convert into withdrawable cash. It's usually expressed as a multiplier, like 20x or 35x, applied either to the bonus amount alone or to the bonus plus your qualifying deposit. Until that cumulative wagering total is met, the bonus balance sits in a locked or restricted state — you can typically play with it, but you can't cash it out, and some operators restrict withdrawals of your own deposited funds too until the requirement clears, depending on how the bonus is structured.

The requirement exists for a straightforward business reason: a casino handing out free money with no strings attached would be trivially exploitable — deposit, claim the bonus, withdraw immediately, repeat. The wagering requirement forces enough real play to happen that the house edge on those games has a chance to work in the operator's favor before any of that promotional money can leave as cash.

How the multiplier is calculated: bonus-only vs. deposit-plus-bonus

The single most consequential piece of fine print in any bonus offer is whether the multiplier applies to the bonus amount alone or to the bonus plus the deposit that triggered it — and it's easy to skim past this distinction because both versions get advertised with a similarly simple-looking headline number.

StructureExampleTotal required wagering
Bonus-only multiplier$100 deposit, $100 bonus, 20x on bonus$2,000
Deposit-plus-bonus multiplier$100 deposit, $100 bonus, 20x on deposit + bonus$4,000

Same deposit, same bonus amount, same multiplier number — and the second structure requires exactly double the wagering. This is why comparing two offers by their headline multiplier alone (both technically "20x") without checking which base amount that multiplier applies to can be genuinely misleading.

Read this line first: whatever else a bonus's terms say, find the sentence that specifies what the multiplier applies to — bonus only, or deposit plus bonus. That single detail can double the real cost of an otherwise identical-looking offer.

Game weighting: why not every bet counts the same

Most operators don't count every dollar wagered equally toward a requirement. Slots commonly count at 100% of the amount wagered, since they typically carry a higher house edge and lower skill component. Table games with a lower house edge and more skill involved — blackjack, video poker, and often baccarat — are frequently weighted much lower, sometimes as little as 5-10%, meaning you'd need to wager $1,000 at a 10% weighting to make the same $100 of progress toward a requirement that a slot session would clear in a single $100 bet. Some game categories, particularly live dealer tables, are excluded from counting toward wagering requirements entirely. This weighting exists for the same underlying reason the requirement itself exists: a game with a near-even house edge and real skill involved (like blackjack played with basic strategy) lets a player churn through wagering with comparatively little expected loss, so operators discount its contribution or exclude it outright to protect the intended economics of the promotion.

A worked example

Take a $50 deposit matched with a $50 bonus, subject to a 25x requirement applied to the bonus amount only, with slots weighted at 100% and table games weighted at 10%. The required wagering is 25 × $50 = $1,250. Playing entirely on slots, that means $1,250 in total wagers — a realistic amount to clear over a number of sessions depending on bet size. Playing entirely on a 10%-weighted blackjack table, the same $1,250 target would require $12,500 in actual wagers, since only a tenth of each bet counts. In practice, most players clear these requirements through a mix of games, but the arithmetic shows why the game you choose to play out a bonus matters as much as the multiplier itself — a bonus that looks easy to clear on paper can become impractical if the games you actually enjoy are weighted low or excluded.

Time limits and other conditions that matter as much as the multiplier

The multiplier and game weighting get the most attention, but several other conditions are just as capable of making a bonus worth far less than it appears. A time limit — commonly somewhere between 7 and 30 days — forfeits the remaining bonus balance and any unwagered progress if the full requirement isn't met before it expires. A maximum bet cap while a bonus is active means placing a single wager above a set amount (sometimes as low as $5-10) can void the bonus and any winnings tied to it, even if the wagering total is nearly met. A maximum cashout cap, common on no-deposit bonuses specifically, limits how much of the winnings generated from bonus play can actually be withdrawn regardless of how much you technically won — so a lucky run on a small no-deposit bonus might still only pay out a capped amount like $100, even if the account balance shows more. Reading through all of these before opting in — not just the headline multiplier — is the only reliable way to know what an offer is actually worth.

Frequently asked questions

Does a lower wagering requirement number always mean a better bonus?

Not necessarily — a low multiplier applied to deposit-plus-bonus can require more total wagering than a higher multiplier applied to the bonus alone, and game weighting, time limits, and cashout caps can change the real value just as much as the headline number.

Why are slots usually weighted higher than table games toward a wagering requirement?

Slots generally carry a higher house edge and no skill component, so operators can count them fully without much risk of a player grinding through a bonus with minimal expected loss — table games with lower house edges and real skill involved are often weighted down to preserve the intended economics of the offer.

What happens if a wagering requirement isn't met before the time limit expires?

Typically the remaining bonus balance and any winnings still attributed to it are forfeited, and any withdrawal restrictions tied to that bonus are lifted only after it's removed from the account — the specific outcome depends on the operator's written terms.

Should I calculate the total wagering amount before accepting any bonus?

It's a reasonable habit — multiplying the requirement base (bonus only, or deposit plus bonus) by the stated multiplier gives you the real number to compare against how much you actually intend to play, rather than judging an offer by its advertised size alone.
